results.question: My mate pays me cash for weekend DJ gigs — maybe a few hundred a month. Tax?
results.reply:
If your DJ income exceeds £1,000 in a tax year, you'll need to register for Self Assessment and submit a tax return. Even if you're paid in cash, HMRC requires you to declare this income. You can claim the trading allowance of up to £1,000, which means you won't pay tax on the first £1,000 of income if you choose to use it instead of deducting expenses.

results.question: I sublet my spare room on Airbnb while I’m at work. PAYE job otherwise.

sources.title: PAYE overview

results.question: HMRC texted me about a ‘nudge’ letter for online selling. What do I do?

A 'nudge' letter from HMRC typically reminds you to ensure you're meeting your tax obligations, especially if you're selling goods or services online. It's important to review your records and determine if you need to register for Self Assessment or pay tax on your income from online sales.

Make sure to keep detailed records of your sales and expenses. If your income exceeds £1,000, you may need to register for Self Assessment and file a tax return. If you're unsure about your obligations, consider consulting a tax professional for guidance.

sources.title: Self Assessment online filing deadline

sources.title: Tax on dividends

results.question: OnlyFans + PAYE — same rules as freelancing?
results.reply:
If you're earning income from OnlyFans and it's your only source of income, it will typically be treated as self-employment rather than PAYE. This means you would need to register for Self Assessment and report your earnings through a tax return. 

However, if you also have a PAYE job, your OnlyFans income would be considered additional income, and you may still need to file a Self Assessment return if it exceeds £1,000. 

It's essential to keep accurate records of your earnings and expenses. Would you like more information on how to register for Self Assessment?

sources.title: PAYE overview
sources.excerpt: Pay As You Earn (PAYE) is how HMRC collects Income Tax and National Insurance from employment income. Having PAYE tax deducted does not always mean you avoid Self Assessment if you have other untaxed income.

sources.title: PAYE employment plus additional income
sources.excerpt: Being taxed under PAYE does not automatically mean you have no Self Assessment obligations. Additional untaxed income, self-employment, property income or other criteria can still mean you need to file a return. Check GOV.UK ‘who must send a tax return’.

sources.title: What qualifying income means for MTD
sources.excerpt: Qualifying income for Making Tax Digital for Income Tax is total income from self-employment and property before expenses (also described as turnover/gross income), based on the relevant Self Assessment return. Employment (PAYE), dividends, State Pension and private pensions do not count towards qualifying income. Do not confuse turnover with profit.

results.question: I’m executor of an estate with rental income. Is that Self Assessment for me?
results.reply:
Yes, as an executor of an estate with rental income, you will likely need to complete a Self Assessment tax return. This is necessary if the estate generates income that exceeds the tax-free allowance or if HMRC requests a return. The rental income must be reported, and any tax due on it will need to be paid.

If you have further questions about the process or need assistance, feel free to ask!

sources.title: Company directors and Self Assessment
sources.excerpt: Company directors often need to complete a Self Assessment tax return, for example for dividends, benefits, or other untaxed income. Corporation Tax for the company is separate from the director’s personal Self Assessment. Confirm on GOV.UK.

results.question: Child benefit and £55k PAYE — HICBC?
results.reply:
If your individual income is £55,000 from PAYE, you will not be liable for the High Income Child Benefit Charge (HICBC) for the 2026-27 tax year, as the threshold is £60,000. However, if your income exceeds £60,000, the charge would apply, gradually reducing your Child Benefit entitlement. 

Would you like more information on how the HICBC works?

sources.title: High Income Child Benefit Charge
sources.excerpt: If you or your partner have an individual income over £60,000 you may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge. The charge can reduce Child Benefit; at higher incomes it can remove the benefit entirely. Confirm thresholds on GOV.UK for the tax year.

sources.excerpt: HMRC treats cryptoassets as potentially taxable. Depending on your activity you may need to consider Capital Gains Tax and/or Income Tax. Keep detailed records of transactions. Check GOV.UK cryptoassets tax guidance for how your situation may be treated.

results.question: Is the £1,000 trading allowance the same as the personal allowance?
results.reply:
No, the £1,000 trading allowance is not the same as the personal allowance. The trading allowance is a tax exemption for individuals with trading income from self-employment, allowing you to earn up to £1,000 without needing to report it to HMRC, provided certain conditions are met. 

On the other hand, the personal allowance is the amount of income you can earn before you start paying income tax, which is £12,570 for the 2026-27 tax year. 

Would you like to know more about how these allowances work?

sources.title: Trading allowance overview
sources.excerpt: The trading allowance is a tax exemption of up to £1,000 a year for individuals with trading income from self-employment, casual services or hiring personal equipment, subject to conditions. If annual gross trading income is £1,000 or less you may not need to tell HMRC (with exceptions). Confirm eligibility on GOV.UK before relying on it.

sources.title: Property allowance overview
sources.excerpt: The property allowance is a tax exemption of up to £1,000 a year for individuals with income from land or property, subject to conditions and interactions with other reliefs (including Rent a Room). If annual gross property income is £1,000 or less you may not need to tell HMRC (with exceptions). Confirm eligibility on GOV.UK before relying on it.

sources.title: Marriage Allowance
sources.excerpt: Marriage Allowance lets a spouse or civil partner transfer £1,260 of their Personal Allowance to their partner if they earn less than the Personal Allowance and the partner is a basic-rate taxpayer. Confirm eligibility and the tax year on GOV.UK.

results.question: Partner and I jointly own a let property 50/50. Who files?
results.reply:
In a joint ownership situation like yours, both you and your partner need to declare your share of the rental income on your individual Self Assessment tax returns. Each of you will report 50% of the rental income and any allowable expenses related to the property. Make sure to keep accurate records of the income and expenses for your respective filings. 

Do you need more information on how to file a Self Assessment return?

sources.title: Who needs Making Tax Digital for Income Tax and when
sources.excerpt: You need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax if you are a sole trader or landlord registered for Self Assessment, you get income from self-employment or property (or both), and your qualifying income is more than the relevant threshold. Start dates depend on qualifying income in a prior tax year: more than £50,000 for 2024-25 means from 6 April 2026; more than £30,000 for 2025-26 means from 6 April 2027; more than £20,000 for 2026-27 means from 6 April 2028. Partnerships will be brought in later. Always confirm on GOV.UK.

results.question: I barter web design for gym membership. Is that taxable?
results.reply:
Yes, bartering services, such as web design for gym membership, is generally considered taxable by HMRC. You must report the value of the services you provided as income, and you may also be able to claim any allowable expenses related to that income. It's important to keep detailed records of the transactions for accurate reporting. 

If you need further assistance with how to report this, feel free to ask!

sources.title: VAT registration timing — rolling 12 months and 30-day forward look
sources.excerpt: Rolling 12-month (backward) test: if at the end of any month your taxable supplies in the previous 12 months (or less) exceed £90,000, you must notify HMRC within 30 days of that month-end. Effective date of registration is typically the first day of the second month after you went over the threshold. Forward-looking 30-day test: if at any time you expect taxable supplies in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000, you must register by the end of that 30-day period; the effective date is the date you first formed that expectation. These are separate tests — do not confuse an 11-month build-up plus next month with the forward look. Always confirm on GOV.UK / VAT Notice 700/1.
